lead: Tea tree extract and tea tree oil come from the leaves of Melaleuca alternifolia, a tree of the myrtle family native to southeast Queensland and northeast New South Wales, Australia.[1][8] The oil, and extracts used in cleansers, toners and blemish products, is used by people who want clearer, calmer skin, mainly on acne-prone and oily complexions and on dandruff-prone scalps.[1]

The best-known active component is terpinen-4-ol, which makes up roughly 35-48% of the oil under the ISO 4730 standard and has antimicrobial activity in laboratory tests.[1] Cosmetic regulators and safety panels treat tea tree-derived ingredients as skin-conditioning agents; a 2026 safety assessment by the Expert Panel for Cosmetic Ingredient Safety concluded that eight tea tree-derived ingredients are safe in cosmetics at current use levels when formulated to be non-sensitizing.[9]

Published human evidence concerns the oil rather than the extract. A 2015 Cochrane review, as summarised on Wikipedia, found one low-quality trial of tea tree oil for acne, and the oil can irritate skin, trigger allergy (more so when oxidised) and is highly toxic if swallowed.[1]

angle.text: People apply tea tree products to spots and oily skin hoping to reduce blemish-causing microbes and inflammation so the skin looks clearer. Most products are low-concentration washes or gels; the oil itself is a stronger preparation that is typically diluted in a base.

paras: Melaleuca alternifolia grows to about 7 m with a bushy crown and papery bark, and its narrow leaves are rich in oil. The species was described by Joseph Maiden and Ernst Betche in 1905 as a variety of M. linariifolia and raised to species rank by Edwin Cheel in 1925.[8] Indigenous Australians of eastern inland areas inhaled the oils of crushed leaves for coughs and colds, applied leaves and poultices to wounds, and drank leaf infusions for sore throats and skin ailments.[8]

Tea tree oil is pale yellow to nearly colourless with a camphor-like scent. ISO 4730 defines it by terpinen-4-ol, gamma-terpinene and alpha-terpinene content, and its composition changes as it oxidises on air exposure; adverse reactions are reduced when eucalyptol (1,8-cineole) content is lower.[1] Water-soluble tea tree extracts are a different preparation; one laboratory study loaded water-soluble extract and hydrophobic oil into separate nanofibre layers and found the extract contributed antioxidant activity while the oil contributed the antibacterial activity.[4]

Commercial production of tea tree oil began in the 1920s, after the chemist Arthur Penfold reported its antiseptic properties; large plantations, mainly in New South Wales, followed in the 1970s and 1980s, and other Melaleuca species are now grown in places such as Tunisia, Egypt and Malaysia.[1] Tea tree extract later became a common botanical in soothing and blemish-care cosmetics; a 2008 Korean patent, for example, lists it among soothing ingredients in a skin-care formulation.[2]

Tea tree oil is promoted for dandruff, acne, lice, scabies, insect bites, and fungal or bacterial skin infections.[1] In cosmetics, tea tree-derived ingredients are classed mainly as skin-conditioning agents in cleansers, toners and treatment products.[9]

Outside skin care, tea tree extract has been tested as a corrosion inhibitor for steel and as an antioxidant and antibacterial load in nanofibre membranes, and the oil has been reviewed as a low-risk biopesticide.[3][4][12] The European Medicines Agency's committee considers traditional topical use plausible for minor wounds, insect bites and small boils but advises against use in children under 12.[1]

Wikipedia, citing a 2015 Cochrane review, says evidence for acne is limited to one low-quality trial of the oil, and that the oil is not recommended for nail fungus or for head lice in children and is unproven against demodex mites.[1] The literature on extract as distinct from oil is much smaller.

Swallowing the oil is highly toxic and can cause serious neurological and gastrointestinal effects; in Australia it is among the essential oils most often involved in poisonings, mostly in children.[1] Skin use can cause irritation and allergic reactions, more often when the oil has oxidised, and the cosmetic safety panel noted oxidised oil could be a sensitizer and advised manufacturers to minimise oxidation.[1][9]

Wikipedia also reports possible hormonal effects, including breast enlargement in men and prepubertal children, and notes a 2018 NIEHS study that identified four constituents as endocrine disruptors; high-dose topical exposure has harmed dogs and cats.[1] The oil is not an approved drug in the US but is used in skin care, and Australia approves it as a complementary medicine for aromatherapy.[1]

Small registered trials of tea tree oil include a 2012 pilot study of a gel for facial acne in 18 participants, trials in chronic blepharitis (34 participants, begun 2009) and seborrhoeic blepharitis (49 participants, tea tree oil swabs versus baby shampoo, begun 2018), a 60-person eyelid demodex study, and a 2021 trial in 30 people on burn healing.[5][6][7][10][11] A Cochrane review summarised on Wikipedia found one low-quality acne trial.[1] No clinical trial of tea tree extract (as distinct from oil) for skin was found.

name: Tea tree extract

card.summary: An Australian antibacterial botanical common in acne products; the oil has limited acne evidence, the extract has almost none.
card.note: Oil is toxic if swallowed and can cause skin allergy.

quick.overview:
Tea tree extract and oil come from an Australian shrub and are common in acne and blemish products for their antibacterial reputation.

A Cochrane review summarised on Wikipedia found one low-quality acne trial favouring the oil. Trials specific to the extract were not found.
quick.mechanism: The oil's main component is terpinen-4-ol, which has antimicrobial activity in lab tests.
quick.risks: Skin irritation and allergy occur, especially with oxidised oil. Swallowing is highly toxic, and a possible link to breast enlargement has been reported.
